summary: Specifies how a WebRTC data channel can serve as a transport for the Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP), and how SDP offer/answer negotiates it. This allows chat and file transfer using MSRP in a WebRTC setting. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: This document lets instant messages and file sharing ride along inside the message lane of a web video call, so one connection can do both.

subtitle: How chat and file transfer using MSRP can ride inside a WebRTC data channel instead of a TCP or TLS connection.

tldr.problem: MSRP was defined for TCP, TLS and a WebSocket subprotocol, but not for the data channels that WebRTC applications use alongside voice and video.
tldr.mechanism: An MSRP data channel is a WebRTC data channel whose subprotocol is msrp. It is negotiated with SDP offer/answer using the dcmap and dcsa attributes, and each MSRP chunk travels in one SCTP user message.
tldr.outcome: Chat, image sharing and file transfer can share one WebRTC connection with other media, and a gateway can link such an endpoint to a classic MSRP endpoint on TCP or TLS. The RFC updates RFC 4975 to allow the msrps scheme over DTLS.

today: RFC 8873 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4975. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why MSRP Over Data Channels
sections.content:
The Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP, RFC 4975) carries a series of related instant messages in a session. It can also be used for image sharing or file transfer. It was first defined for TCP and TLS connections, and later for a WebSocket subprotocol.

This RFC defines an MSRP data channel: a WebRTC data channel for which the subprotocol is msrp and which is negotiated with the SDP offer/answer mechanism. The TCP and TLS layers are not used.

The listed benefits are a proven messaging protocol for applications, integration with WebRTC voice, video and data, reuse of the SDP negotiation MSRP already has, and interworking with MSRP endpoints on TCP or TLS. Compared with WebSocket, data channels offer low-latency transport, NAT-aware connectivity and the security features of WebRTC.
sections.plainLanguage: MSRP is a way to send chat messages and files. This document says how to send them through the side lane of a web call, so one connection can do many jobs.

sections.title: The Data Channel Properties
sections.content:
An MSRP data channel has fixed WebRTC data channel properties. The subprotocol identifier is msrp, transmission is reliable and in-order, and the label is set by the MSRP application.

Each MSRP session maps to exactly one data channel. A file transfer session also maps to one data channel, and that channel MAY be reused for another file transfer once the first is complete.
sections.plainLanguage: The lane is set up so nothing gets lost and everything arrives in order, like a conveyor belt. Each conversation gets its own belt.

sections.title: Negotiating With SDP
sections.content:
Each offer and answer MUST include a dcmap attribute in the media description for the SCTP association. It carries label= and subprotocol="msrp". The max-retr and max-time parameters MUST NOT be included, and if ordered is included it MUST be true.

MSRP-specific attributes are embedded using dcsa attributes. Offers and answers MUST include path, msrp-cema and setup, and omitting one is a protocol error. They MAY include accept-types, accept-wrapped-types, max-size, the direction attributes (sendonly, recvonly, inactive, sendrecv) and the file transfer attributes from RFC 5547.

The path attribute is not used to route messages, because the channel is set up by offer/answer. This is similar to MSRP CEMA (RFC 6714), which is why msrp-cema is mandatory. An endpoint still MUST perform the MSRP URI comparison from RFC 4975 on received messages.

The embedded setup attribute chooses which endpoint takes the active MSRP role. It has no relationship with the DTLS connection roles.

The MSRP URI gains a new transport value, dc. The scheme in the URI is always msrps, because data channels are always secured with DTLS.
sections.plainLanguage: Before chatting, both sides swap a form saying what they can do and which side starts. The form has some boxes that must be filled in and some that are optional.

sections.title: Opening, Framing and Closing
sections.content:
Normal MSRP procedures from RFC 4975 apply unless this RFC says otherwise. Once the data channel opens, the active endpoint opens the MSRP session by sending an MSRP SEND message, empty or not, to the passive peer.

Each text-based MSRP message is sent using standard MSRP framing and chunking, with each chunk delivered in a single SCTP user message. So every chunk MUST be no longer than the peer's max-message-size value.

An MSRP session is closed by closing its data channel. The port in the m= line SHOULD NOT be set to zero for this, because that would close the whole SCTP association and affect every data channel. Where RFC 4975 would set the port to zero, the offerer instead removes the matching dcmap and dcsa attributes. If the channel fails, the session is considered failed, and an endpoint MAY try to negotiate a new one.
sections.plainLanguage: The side that goes first knocks to start the chat. Each piece of message has to fit in one envelope. To end the chat, you close that one lane without shutting down the whole road.

sections.title: Gateways to Classic MSRP
sections.content:
A gateway can connect a data channel endpoint to an MSRP endpoint that uses TLS over TCP in two ways. As an MSRP back-to-back user agent it handles all procedures itself, and this RFC adds nothing for that model. Or it can do transport-level interworking.

For transport-level interworking the gateway MUST use MSRP CEMA toward the non-data-channel endpoint. If that endpoint does not support CEMA, the gateway must act as a back-to-back user agent. The gateway MUST NOT modify the path or setup values it receives. An endpoint using data channel transport MUST NOT request any relays, although it MAY interoperate with a peer that signals relays.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway is a translator between two people who speak different dialects. It either rewrites everything or just passes the notes along without changing them.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
Confidentiality, integrity and source authentication for MSRP over data channels come from the WebRTC data channel security in RFC 8831. RFC 4975 still allows MSRP over nonsecured TCP and has no way to guarantee TLS end to end, since TCP might be used on some hops. Operators need policies to ensure traffic is protected between endpoints.

The RFC points to RFC 5547 for file transfer security, RFC 7092 for back-to-back user agents, and Section 14.5 of RFC 4975 on message attribution to remote identities. If SIP carries the offer/answer, the SIP security considerations apply.
sections.plainLanguage: The data lane is locked by default. But if a message later leaves for an old unlocked road, the people running the system must make sure it stays protected.

sections.title: Updates to RFC 4975 and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC updates RFC 4975 by allowing the msrps scheme when the underlying connection is protected with DTLS.

IANA added a reference to this RFC for the msrps URI scheme and for the msrp subprotocol identifier. It also added the usage level dcsa (msrp) to the registrations of the SDP attributes that may appear in an MSRP data channel, such as accept-types, path and msrp-cema.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule book gets one small change, and the official lists get a note about the new way to use these names.
